Let $f:X\\rightarrow Y$ be a morphism of schemes, let\n$y\\in Y$ and $\\kappa(y)$ the residue field of $y$ with the inclusion\nmorphism being $\\iota: \\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\:\\kappa(y)\\rightarrow Y$.\nWe define the **fibre of $f$ at $y$** to be the scheme\n$X_y := X\\times_Y \\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\:\\kappa(y)$\n:::\n\n### Quasi-coherent Sheaves {#annexe_quasi_coherent}\n\nSo far we have introduced schemes and morphisms between them without\nmentioning any sheaves other than the structure sheaves, our review of\nscheme theory would not be complete without mentioning sheaves of\nmodules.\n\n::: definition\n**Definition 331**. Let $X$ be a scheme and $\\mathcal{O}_X$ its\nstructure sheaf. A **sheaf of modules** on $X$, also called a sheaf of\n$\\mathcal{O}_X$-modules is a sheaf $\\mathcal{F}$ on $X$ such that\n$\\mathcal{F}(U)$ is an $\\mathcal{O}_X(U)$-module for all open subsets\n$U\\subset X$ and all restriction maps are $\\mathcal{O}_X$-modules\nhomomorphisms in the sense that\n$$(\\varphi +\\psi)\\vert_U = \\varphi\\vert_U + \\psi\\vert_U \\: \\text{ and }\\: (\\lambda\\varphi)\\vert_U = \\lambda\\vert_U\\cdot \\varphi\\vert_U$$\nfor all open subsets $U\\subset V$ of $X$, $\\lambda\\in \\mathcal{O}_X(V)$\nand $\\varphi,\\psi\\in\\mathcal{F}(V)$.\n:::\n\n::: examples\n**Examples 332**.\n\n- Let $X$ be a scheme, then $\\mathcal{O}_X$ is a sheaf of modules on\n  $X$.\n\n- Let $f:\\mathcal{F}\\rightarrow \\mathcal{G}$ be a morphisms of sheaves\n  on a scheme $X$. For any open subset $U\\subset X$, we set\n  $(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ker}}f)(U):= \\ker( f_U : \\mathcal{F}(U) \\rightarrow \\mathcal{G}(U) )$.\n  $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ker}}f$ is a sheaf of modules on $X$, we call it the\n  **kernel sheaf** of $f$.\n\n- For a morphism $f:\\mathcal{F}\\rightarrow \\mathcal{G}$ of sheaves on a\n  scheme $X$ and any open subset $U\\subset X$, we set\n  $(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Im}}' f)(U):= \\mathop{\\mathrm{im}}( f_U : \\mathcal{F}(U) \\rightarrow\\mathcal{G}(U)).$\n  $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Im}}' f$ defines a presheaf of modules but not yet a\n  sheaf. We define its sheafification $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Im}}f$ the\n  **image sheaf** of $f$.\n\n- Let $f:\\mathcal{F}\\rightarrow \\mathcal{G}$ be a morphism of sheaves on\n  a scheme $X$. We define the **tensor presheaf**\n  $\\mathcal{F}\\otimes'\\mathcal{G}$ on $X$ by\n  $(\\mathcal{F}\\otimes'\\mathcal{G})(U):= \\mathcal{F}(U) \\otimes_{\\mathcal{O}_X(U)}\\mathcal{G}(U)$\n  for any open subset $U\\subset X$. We define its sheafification to be\n  the **tensor sheaf** $\\mathcal{F}\\otimes \\mathcal{G}$.\n\n- Let $f:X\\rightarrow Y$ be a morphism of schemes and let $\\mathcal{F}$\n  be a sheaf on $X$. Consider the direct image sheaf $f_*\\mathcal{F}$ on\n  $Y$, it is a sheaf of $\\mathcal{O}_Y$-modules.\n:::\n\n::: {#exact_at_level_of_stalk .lemma}\n**Lemma 333**. *Let $(X, \\mathcal{O}_X)$ be a ringed space. The category\n$\\mathop{\\mathrm{\\bf{Mod}}}(\\mathcal{O}_X)$ is an abelian category.\nMoreover a complex\n$\\dots \\rightarrow\\mathcal{F}_1\\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_2 \\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_3 \\rightarrow\\dots$\nis exact at $\\mathcal{F}_2$ if and only if for all $x\\in X$, the complex\n$\\dots \\rightarrow(\\mathcal{F}_1)_x\\rightarrow (\\mathcal{F}_2)_x \\rightarrow (\\mathcal{F}_3)_x \\rightarrow\\dots$\nis exact at $(\\mathcal{F}_2)_x$.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@Stacks] [(Tag\n01AG)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01AG) ◻\n:::\n\nWe now describe exactly how an $R$-module $M$ determines a sheaf of\nmodules $\\widetilde{M}$ on the affine scheme\n$X=\\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\:R$\n\n::: definition\n**Definition 334**. Let $X=\\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\: R$ be an affine\nscheme, and let $M$ be an $R$-module. For any open subset $U\\subset X$,\nwe set $$\\begin{equation*}\n    \\begin{split}\n        \\widetilde{M}(U) := \\{\\varphi = (\\varphi_P)_{P\\in U} \\mid& \\varphi_P \\in M_P,\\:\\forall P\\in U,\\\\\n        &\\forall P, \\:\\exists U_P \\text{ an open neighbourhood of } P \\text{ in } U\\\\\n        &\\text{and } g\\in M, f\\in R \\text{ with } \\varphi_Q = \\frac{g}{f}, \\:\\forall Q\\in U_P\n    \\end{split}\n\\end{equation*}$$ From the definition, $\\widetilde{M}$ is a sheaf,\nmoreover $\\widetilde{M}(U)$ is a module over\n$\\widetilde{R}(U) = \\mathcal{O}_X(U)$, hence $\\widetilde{M}$ is a sheaf\nof modules on $X$. We call it the **sheaf associated to $M$**.\n:::\n\n::: proposition\n**Proposition 335**. *Let $R$ be a ring, let $M$ be an $R$-module, and\nlet $\\widetilde{M}$ be the sheaf on $X : \\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\: R$\nassociated to $M$. Then :*\n\n- *$\\widetilde{M}$ is an $\\mathcal{O}_X$-module,*\n\n- *for each $P\\in X$, the stalk $(\\widetilde{M})_P$ of the sheaf\n  $\\widetilde{M}$ at $P$ is isomorphic to the localized module $M_P$\n  and*\n\n- *in particular the global sections $\\widetilde{M}(X) = M$.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne] Proposition $5.1$. ◻\n:::\n\n::: definition\n**Definition 336**. A sheaf of modules $\\mathcal{F}$ on a scheme $X$ is\nsaid to be **locally free** if there is an affine open cover\n$\\{U_i |i\\in I\\}$ of $X$ such that on every open\n$U_i = \\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\:R_i$ the restricted sheaf\n$\\mathcal{F}\\vert_{U_i}$ is isomorphic to the sheaf $\\widetilde{M}_i$\nassociated to a free $R_i$-module $M_i$ of finite rank. If this rank is\nthe same for all $i\\in I$, it is also called the rank of $\\mathcal{F}$.\n:::\n\nBut not every sheaf of modules on an affine scheme\n$\\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\: R$ is associate to an $R$-module. For that\nreason, we have to define additional properties.\n\n::: definition\n**Definition 337**. A sheaf of modules $\\mathcal{F}$ on a scheme $X$ is\ncalled **quasi-coherent** if there is an affine cover $\\{ U_i |i\\in I\\}$\nof $X$ such that on every open $U_i=\\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\:R_i$, the\nrestricted sheaf $\\mathcal{F}\\vert_{U_i}$ is isomorphic to the sheaf\nassociated to $M_i$ and $R_i$-module. Moreover, if $M_i$ is a finitely\ngenerated $R_i$-module for all $i$, we say that $\\mathcal{F}$ is a\n$\\textbf{coherent}$ sheaf\n:::\n\n::: example\n**Example 338**. The structure sheaf $\\mathcal{O}_X$ is quasi-coherent\non any scheme $X$, since for any open subset\n$U=\\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\:R\\subset X$ is in fact of the form\n$\\mathcal{F}\\vert_U \\cong \\widetilde{M}$ for any $R$-module $M$\n:::\n\nWe define the **tensor product**\n$\\mathcal{F}\\otimes_{\\mathcal{O}_X}\\mathcal{G}$ of two\n$\\mathcal{O}_X$-modules to be the sheaf associated to the presheaf\n$U\\mapsto \\mathcal{F}(U) \\otimes_{\\mathcal{O}_X(U)} \\mathcal{G}(U)$.\n\nTaking the tensor product of two quasi-coherent sheaves gives a\nquasi-coherent sheaf again\n\n::: proposition\n**Proposition 339**. *Let $f:X\\rightarrow Y$ be a morphism of schemes\nwith $X$ a Noetherian scheme. Then is $\\mathcal{F}$ is a quasi-coherent\nsheaf of $\\mathcal{O}_X$-modules, then its direct image $f_*\\mathcal{F}$\nis a quasi-coherent sheaf of $\\mathcal{O}_Y$-modules.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne], Proposition $II.\\:5.8$. ◻\n:::\n\nUnfortunately, the adjoint functor $f^{-1}$ from Remark\n[305](#almost_pullback_sheaf){reference-type=\"ref\"\nreference=\"almost_pullback_sheaf\"} does not take quasi-coherent sheaves\non $X$ to quasi-coherent sheaves on $Y$. For that reason we define the\n*pull-back sheaf* $f^*$ as follow\n\n::: definition\n**Definition 340**. Let\n$f:(X,\\mathcal{O}_X)\\rightarrow (Y,\\mathcal{O}_Y)$ be a morphism of\nringed spaces and $\\mathcal{G}$ a sheaf on $Y$. We define the\n**pull-back sheaf** $f^*\\mathcal{G}$ to be the tenor product\n$f^{-1}\\mathcal{G}\\otimes_{f^{-1}\\mathcal{O}_Y} \\mathcal{O}_X$\n:::\n\nAnd now the pull-back sheaf of a quasi-coherent sheaf is again\nquasi-coherent by Proposition $II.\\:5.8$ from [@Hartshorne].\n\n::: construction\n**Construction 341**. Let $\\mathcal{F}$ be a sheaf on a scheme $X$. For\na closed point $P\\in X$ and the inclusion map $i:P\\rightarrow X$, the\nsheaf pull-back sheaf $i^*\\mathcal{F}$ on $P$ has only one non-trivial\nspace of sections $i^*\\mathcal{F}(P)$. The geometric meaning of this\nspace is better seen in the affine case. Let\n$X = \\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\: R$ so that $P\\trianglelefteq R$ is a\nmaximal ideal and $\\mathcal{F} = \\widetilde{M}$ for an $R$-module $M$.\nWe have $i^*\\mathcal{F}(P) = M\\otimes_R R/P = M/PM$ as a vector space\nover the residue field $\\kappa(P)$. This vector space\n$i^*\\mathcal{F}(P)$ over $\\kappa(P)$ is called the **fibre** of\n$\\mathcal{F}$ at $P$.\n:::\n\n::: theorem\n**Theorem 342**. *The category of quasi-coherent sheaves on schemes is\nan abelian category.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne], $III.\\: 1.0.5$. ◻\n:::\n\nIn particular it is stable under kernels, images, cokernels and\nquotients.\\\nRegarding Lemma [333](#exact_at_level_of_stalk){reference-type=\"ref\"\nreference=\"exact_at_level_of_stalk\"}, we have the following proposition.\n\n::: proposition\n**Proposition 343**. *If\n$0\\rightarrow\\mathcal{F}_1\\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_2 \\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_3\\rightarrow 0$\nis a short exact sequence of quasi-coherent sheaf on an affine scheme\nscheme $X$, then\n$0\\rightarrow\\mathcal{F}_1(X)\\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_2(X) \\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_3(X)\\rightarrow 0$\nis a short exact sequence. In other words, the global section functor is\nflat*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne], Proposition $5.6$. ◻\n:::\n\nHowever it is not the case that the global section functor is flat for\nnon-affine schemes, it is only left exact. Indeed the category of\nquasi-coherent sheaves has *enough injectives*, which means that all of\nits objects admit an *injective resolution* which basically mean that\nthe above global section functor is left exact. This follows from the\nfollowing result\n\n::: proposition\n**Proposition 344**. *Let $(X,\\mathcal{O}_S$ be a ringed space. Then the\ncategory of sheaves of $\\mathcal{O}_X$-modules has enough injectives.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* [@Hartshorne] Proposition $III.\\: 2.2$. ◻\n:::\n\nNakayama's Lemma [255](#Nakayama_first_lemma){reference-type=\"ref\"\nreference=\"Nakayama_first_lemma\"} is a useful tool in algebraic\ngeometry. It has the following interpretation in terms of coherent\nsheaves\n\n::: corollary\n**Corollary 345** (Coherent Nakayama). *If the stalk of a coherent sheaf\nis zero at a point $P$, then the sheaf restricts to zero in an open\nneighbourhood of $P$.*\n:::\n\n::: {#ideal_sheaf .lemma}\n**Lemma 346**. *Let $i: X \\rightarrow Y$ be a closed embedding. Then*\n\n- *If $\\mathcal{F}$ is a quasi-coherent sheaf on $X$, then the direct\n  image $i_*\\mathcal{F}$ is a quasi-coherent sheaf on $Y$.*\n\n- *$0 \\rightarrow \\mathcal{I}_{X/Y} \\rightarrow\\mathcal{O}_{Y}\\rightarrow i_*\\mathcal{O}_X\\rightarrow0$\n  is an exact sequence of quasi-coherent sheaves with\n  $\\mathcal{I}_{X/Y}$ the kernel of\n  $i^{\\#}:\\mathcal{O}_Y\\rightarrow i_*\\mathcal{O}_X$ called the ideal\n  sheaf of $X$ in $Y$.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne], Proposition $5.9$. ◻\n:::\n\n::: {#affine_morph_quasi_coherent .proposition}\n**Proposition 347**. *There is an anti-equivalence between the category\nof affine morphisms $X\\rightarrow Y$ and the category of quasi-coherent\nsheaves of $\\mathcal{O}_X$-algebras.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@Stacks] [(Tag\n01SA)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01SA).\\\n ◻\n:::\n\n### Quasi-Coherent Sheaf Cohomology {#Sheaf_cohomology}\n\nWe have seen above that the functor of global sections (which can be\nthought of as a derived functor here) sends a short exact sequence\n$$0\\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_1 \\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_2 \\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_3 \\rightarrow 0$$\nof quasi-coherent sheaves on a scheme $X$ to the following left exact\nsequence\n$$0\\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_1(X) \\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_2(X) \\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_3(X) \\rightarrow \\dots$$\nSheaf cohomology is basically the study of when the above sequence fails\nto be exact.\n\n::: definition\n**Definition 348**. Let $\\mathcal{F}$ be a quasi-coherent sheaf on $X$\nand $\\{U_1,...,U_n\\}$ an affine open cover of $X$.\n\n- For all $p\\in \\mathbb{N}$, we define the sets\n  $$C^p(\\mathcal{F}) = \\bigoplus_{i_0<\\dots< i_p} \\mathcal{F}(U_{i_0} \\cap \\dots \\cap U_{i_p})$$\n  An element $\\varphi \\in C^p(\\mathcal{F})$ is just a collection of\n  sections\n  $\\varphi_{i_0,\\dots ,ip}\\in \\mathcal{F}(U_{i_0} \\cap \\dots \\cap U_{i_p})$\n  for all intersections of $p+1$ sets taken from the chosen affine open\n  cover.\n\n- For every $p\\in \\mathbb{N}$ we define a linear **boundary map**\n  $d^p: C^p(\\mathcal{F}) \\rightarrow C^{p+1}(\\mathcal{F})$ by\n  $$(d^p\\varphi)_{i_0,\\dots,i_{p+1}} = \\sum^{p+1}_{k=0} (-1)^k \\varphi_{i_0,\\dots,\\hat{i_k},\\dots, i_{p+1} \\vert_{U_{i_0}\\cap\\dots \\cap U_{i_{p+1}}}}$$\n:::\n\n::: lemma\n**Lemma 349**. *The composition of two consecutive boundary maps is\n$0$.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* This is a straight up computation. ◻\n:::\n\n::: definition\n**Definition 350**. Let $\\mathcal{F}$ be a coherent sheaf on a scheme\n$X$ and let $r\\in \\mathbb{N}$.\n\n- The following chain complex is called the **$\\check{\\textbf{C}}$ech\n  complex** (the fact that it is a complex follows from the previous\n  lemma),\n  $$C^0(\\mathcal{F}) \\xrightarrow[]{d^0} C^1(\\mathcal{F})\\xrightarrow[]{d^1} C^2(\\mathcal{F})\\xrightarrow[]{d^2} \\dots.$$\n\n- We define the $r$-th **$\\check{\\text{C}}$ech cohomology group** of\n  $\\mathcal{F}$ to be\n  $H^r(X,\\mathcal{F}) := \\ker d^r / \\mathop{\\mathrm{im}}d^{r-1}$. With\n  the convention that $C^{-1}(\\mathcal{F})$ and $d^{-1}$ are zero so\n  that $H^0(X,\\mathcal{F}) = \\ker d^0$.\n\n- Suppose we work over a field $k$, we ca define $h^r(X,\\mathcal{F})$\n  the dimension of $H^r(X,\\mathcal{F})$ as a $k$-vector space.\n:::\n\nThe $\\check{\\text{C}}$ech cohomology is usually defined for sheaves of\nabelian groups, but since quasi-coherent sheaves are a special kind of\nsheaf of abelian groups, we make no distinction between quasi-coherent\nsheaf cohomology and the $\\check{\\text{C}}$ech cohomology. It is also\nimportant to note that as we have defined it, the quasi-coherent sheaf\ncohomology is independent of the choice of affine open covering. We have\nthe following first few properties.\n\n::: proposition\n**Proposition 351**. *Let $\\mathcal{F}$ be a quasi-coherent sheaf on a\nscheme $X$. Then*\n\n- *$H^0(X,\\mathcal{F}) = \\mathcal{F}(X)$,*\n\n- *if $X$ is affine, then $H^r(X,\\mathcal{F}) = 0$ for all $r> 0$.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne], for $a)$, Lemma $III.\\: 4.1$ and for $b)$, ◻\n:::\n\n::: proposition\n**Proposition 352**. *Let\n$0\\rightarrow \\mathcal{F}_1\\rightarrow\\mathcal{F}_2\\rightarrow\\mathcal{F}_3\\rightarrow 0$\nbe a short exact sequence of quasi-coherent sheaves on a scheme $X$.\nThen there exists a long exact sequence of cohomology groups\n$$\\begin{equation*}\n    \\begin{split}\n        0&\\rightarrow H^0(X,\\mathcal{F_\\text{1}}) \\rightarrow H^0(X,\\mathcal{F_\\text{2}}) \\rightarrow H^0(X,\\mathcal{F_\\text{3}})\\\\\n        &\\rightarrow H^1(X,\\mathcal{F_\\text{1}}) \\rightarrow H^1(X,\\mathcal{F_\\text{2}}) \\rightarrow H^1(X,\\mathcal{F_\\text{3}})\\\\\n        &\\rightarrow H^2(X,\\mathcal{F_\\text{1}}) \\rightarrow \\dots\n    \\end{split}\n\\end{equation*}$$*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@Vakil] Chapter $18.1$, $(iii)$.\\\n ◻\n:::\n\nWe only mention it, but the cohomology of sheaves gives us powerful\ninvariants, useful for the classification of schemes. Such as, the\ncohomology groups themselves, the *Euler characteristics*, the genus of\na scheme and much more.\n\n### Analytification\n\nA smooth scheme over $\\mathbb{C}$ can be seen as a complex manifold.\nSince we can apply techniques of complex analysis and differential\ngeometry to complex manifolds, provided we have a nice dictionary\nbetween the language of abstract algebraic geometry and complex\nmanifolds, we could translate those analytical results into results\nabout schemes.\n\nWe first need to define what we mean by an analytic space (complex in\nour case)\n\n::: definition\n**Definition 353**. Let $U\\subset \\mathbb{C}^n$ be the Cartesian product\nof open discs : $\\{|z_i| <1 \\mid i=1,...,n\\}$, let $f_1,...,f_m$ be\nholomorphic functions on $U$ and let $Y\\subset U$ be the closed subset\n(for the usual Euclidean topology) consisting of the zero locus\n$V(f_1,...,f_m)$, with its structure sheaf the restriction\n$\\mathcal{O}_Y = \\mathcal{O}_U/(f_1,...,f_m)$ (for $\\mathcal{O}_U$ the\nsheaf of holomorphic functions on $U$).\\\nA **complex analytic space** is a locally ringed space\n$(X,\\mathcal{O}_X)$ which can be covered by affine open sets, each of\nwhich biholomorphic (as locally ringed spaces) to a space $Y$ as above.\n(Notice that $Y$ is open in $X$ but closed in $U\\subset \\mathbb{C}^n$)\n:::\n\nNotice that the sheaf structure is actually a structure of\n$\\mathbb{C}$-modules.\n\n::: remark\n**Remark 50**. Theses spaces are called *analytic* because the topology\non them is the topology induced from the usual one on $\\mathbb{C}^n$\nopen sets are small, and compatible with analysis (limits, continuity,\nholomorphic functions, \\...)\n:::\n\nSimilarly as in the algebraic case, complex analytic spaces are a\ngeneralisation of complex manifolds, indeed, they also allow\nsingularities. For example, let\n$X = \\{(u,v)\\in\\mathbb{C}^2 \\mid uv= 0\\}$ be a complex analytic space,\nthen it is not a complex manifold since there is no neighbourhood at the\norigin that is biholomorphic to an open subset of $\\mathbb{C}$.\n\n::: definition\n**Definition 354**. If $X$ and $Y$ are complex analytical spaces, a\nmorphism $\\varphi:X\\rightarrow Y$ of locally $\\mathbb{C}$-ringed spaces\nis called a **holomorphic map**.\n:::\n\nAs the name of this section suggests, the goal is to associate to an\nalgebraic scheme $X$ over $\\mathbb{C}$ such a complex analytic space\nthat we will denote by $X^{an}$,\n\n::: construction\n**Construction 355**. Let $X$ be a scheme of finite type over\n$\\mathbb{C}$. Consider a covering of $X$ by affine open subsets\n$Y_i=\\mathop{\\mathrm{Spec}}\\:A_i$, recall that for all $i$, $A_i$ is of\nfinite type, so $A_i \\cong \\mathbb{C}[x_1, ..., x_n]/(f_1, ..., f_m)$\nwith $f_1,...,f_m$ polynomials in $x_1,...,x_n$. We can regard those\npolynomials as holomorphic functions on $\\mathbb{C}^n$ and their zero\nlocus form a complex analytic closed subspace $Y_i^{an}$ in\n$\\mathbb{C}^n$. Since the scheme $X$ is obtained by glueing the open\nsets $Y_i$, we can use the same glueing data to glue the analytic spaces\n$Y_i^{an}$ into an analytic space $X^{an}$. This is the associated\ncomplex analytic space of $X$.\n:::\n\n::: remark\n**Remark 51**. Notice that the above construction is functorial thus we\nobtain a functor $\\_^{an}$ from the category of finite schemes over\n$\\mathbb{C}$ to the category of complex analytical spaces. There is also\na continuous map $\\varphi : X^{an}\\rightarrow X$ of the underlying\ntopological spaces, which sends $X^{an}$ bijectively onto closed points\nof $X$.\n:::\n\nIn his groundbreaking paper [@Serre], Serre proved a plethora of results\nabout the relationship between a scheme $X$ ans its associated analytic\nspace $X^{an}$, we enumerate them below:\n\n::: {#analytification_space .proposition}\n**Proposition 356**. *Let $X$ be a scheme over $\\mathbb{C}$, locally of\nfinite type and $X^{an}$ the associated analytical space. Then the\nscheme $X$ is*\n\n- *non-empty,*\n\n- *discrete,*\n\n- *regular,*\n\n- *normal,*\n\n- *reduced, or*\n\n- *of dimension $n$*\n\n*if and only if the associated $X^{an}$ is as well.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@SGA], Proposition $XII.\\:2.1$. ◻\n:::\n\n::: {#analytification_morphisms .proposition}\n**Proposition 357**. *Let $X$ and $Y$ be two schemes over $\\mathbb{C}$\nlocally of finite type, $f:X\\rightarrow Y$ a morphism of finite type and\n$f^{an}: X^{an}\\rightarrow Y^{an}$ the associated analytical morphism\ninduced by $f$. Then $f$ is*\n\n- *surjective,*\n\n- *a closed immersion,*\n\n- *an immersion,*\n\n- *proper, or*\n\n- *finite*\n\n*if and only if $f^{an}$ is as well.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* See [@SGA], Proposition $XII.\\:3.2$. ◻\n:::\n\nWe say that a complex analytical space $(X,\\mathcal{O}_X)$ is actually a\n*Riemann surface* if and only if it is $1$-dimensional and smooth (or\nnon-singular). Thus, notice that the above notions also make sense for\nRiemann surfaces when considering their structure sheaf of holomorphic\nfunctions.\n\n::: remark\n**Remark 52**. It is interesting to note that in [@Serre], for $X$ a\nprojective scheme over $\\mathbb{C}$, Serre also showed that the\nanalytification functor yields an equivalence of categories between\ncoherent sheaves on $X$ and coherent analytic sheaves on $X^{an}$.\n:::\n\n"
  },

      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "\\gamma_1,\\gamma_2 : [0,1] \\rightarrow X",
        "hash": "d764bc643e789449",
        "id": "eq-56",

        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "\\gamma_1(1) = \\gamma_2(0)",
        "hash": "7f2b36d576013f9b",
        "id": "eq-57",

        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "\\gamma_1\\bullet\\gamma_2 : [0,1]\\rightarrow X",
        "hash": "be738c9883dcbdd3",
        "id": "eq-58",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "\\gamma_1\\bullet\\gamma_2 =\n    \\begin{cases}\n      \\gamma_1(2t) & \\text{for $t\\in [0,\\frac{1}{2}]$}\\\\\n      \\gamma_2(2t-1) & \\text{for $t\\in [\\frac{1}{2}, 1]$}.\n    \\end{cases}",
        "hash": "de44843fe8a168d7",
        "id": "eq-59",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "We say that a topological space is **simply-connected** if and only if\nits fundamental group is trivial.\n\n::: remark\n**Remark 1**. Let",
        "hash": "5c8a4d249da59ec8",
        "id": "eq-60",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "be a continuous map between\npointed topological spaces such that",
        "hash": "97fd5b5c9c4d45c2",
        "id": "eq-61",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", then we denote by",
        "hash": "aa5d3097257065d7",
        "id": "eq-62",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "the induced homomorphism, obtained\nby composition,",
        "hash": "bed8ba937043ba5a",
        "id": "eq-63",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "for any",
        "hash": "57ccab62136e84fc",
        "id": "eq-64",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ".\n:::\n\nAs expected, the fundamental group is a topological invariant :\n\n::: proposition\n**Proposition 4**. *Homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental\ngroups. If",
        "hash": "39753a5a90db48ba",
        "id": "eq-65",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is a homeomorphism, then",
        "hash": "832775e9ff2e528f",
        "id": "eq-66",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is an isomorphism.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* If",
        "hash": "e03a26c901b7f421",
        "id": "eq-67",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is a homeomorphism, then",
        "hash": "832775e9ff2e528f",
        "id": "eq-68",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ".\nSimilarly,",
        "hash": "c02adb233f5e5fa5",
        "id": "eq-69",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is the identity on",
        "hash": "155c124d9d21161c",
        "id": "eq-70",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ". ◻\n:::\n\nSimilarly, one proves the following.\n\n::: corollary\n**Corollary 5**. *Two homotopic equivalent spaces have the same\nfundamental group. If",
        "hash": "4f860017069f84c6",
        "id": "eq-71",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is a homotopy equivalence, then",
        "hash": "1de968d3c12bc3f0",
        "id": "eq-72",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is an isomorphism.*\n:::\n\nOne thing to notice is that if",
        "hash": "3331f942f114628f",
        "id": "eq-73",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is not path-connected, the\nfundamental groups based at points in different path-connected\ncomponents don't have any relation to each other. Therefore, it is\ncustomary to consider path-connected topological spaces when studying\nfundamental groups. The next proposition tells us that in a\npath-connected space, the fundamental group is insensitive to changes of\nbase points. Thus, when this is clear, we will sometimes omit to write\nthe base point.\n\n::: {#fund_grou_base_pt .proposition}\n**Proposition 6**. *If",
        "hash": "8f9f66ab867a5844",
        "id": "eq-74",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is a path-connected topological space, then",
        "hash": "3ff660f95e5eb966",
        "id": "eq-75",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "and",
        "hash": "6201111b83a0cb5b",
        "id": "eq-76",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "are isomorphic for any",
        "hash": "9cfc1251252029c2",
        "id": "eq-77",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ".*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* Since two points",
        "hash": "a943742685c0ce0b",
        "id": "eq-78",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "and",
        "hash": "6201111b83a0cb5b",
        "id": "eq-79",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "may be joined by a path",
        "hash": "5a3621a072752105",
        "id": "eq-80",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "starting at",
        "hash": "491013df3b6cce22",
        "id": "eq-81",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "and ending at",
        "hash": "2cfe2fa72ee38daf",
        "id": "eq-82",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ",",
        "hash": "d03502c43d74a30b",
        "id": "eq-83",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is\nnon-canonically isomorphic to",
        "hash": "0656042245d733c8",
        "id": "eq-84",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "via",
        "hash": "4d327af41f96c23c",
        "id": "eq-85",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ". ◻\n:::\n\n::: example\n**Example 7**. Of course, since",
        "hash": "92489af52def59b8",
        "id": "eq-86",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is contractible, any loop\nis homotopic to the constant loop, so",
        "hash": "98332309b93bc46b",
        "id": "eq-87",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "for any base point",
        "hash": "a8cb803a6e2e0d53",
        "id": "eq-88",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ".\n:::\n\nComputing non-trivial fundamental groups such as",
        "hash": "5659a5dfafb9f4e5",
        "id": "eq-89",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is already\nharder. An alternative is to use the theory of covering spaces and\nlifting of paths. The calculation of",
        "hash": "e610671645a11caa",
        "id": "eq-90",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "however, has many\napplications. It allows one to give a proof of the *Fundamental Theorem\nof Algebra*, to show the *Brouwer's fixed-point theorem in dimension",
        "hash": "31ca24f4bcbbd25b",
        "id": "eq-91",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "* or even to prove the *Borsuk-Ulam theorem in dimension",
        "hash": "9e80199ef67dbef7",
        "id": "eq-92",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "* (these\ntheorems with their proofs can be found in [@Hatcher] as Theorem",
        "hash": "ecd20d8787495491",
        "id": "eq-93",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ",",
        "hash": "d03502c43d74a30b",
        "id": "eq-94",
        "mathml": null,

      {
        "canonical_tex": ".\\\n\n### Covering Spaces and their Galois structure {#fund_grp_cov_spaces}\n\nIn this section, we introduce the theory of covering spaces. Then we\nshow that it exhibits a structure that behaves similarly to that of\nfield extensions. Later on, we will prove the existence of a so-called\nuniversal covering that is deeply related to the fundamental group.\n\n[]{#covering_spaces label=\"covering_spaces\"}\n\n::: {#def_cover .definition}\n**Definition 8**. A **covering** of a topological space",

      {
        "canonical_tex": "\\begin{split}\n        \\text{$L|k$ is Galois} &\\Leftrightarrow  \\forall\\sigma\\in G, \\sigma(L) = L,\\\\\n        &\\Leftrightarrow \\text{there exist a map } .\\vert_L:G\\rightarrow\\mathop{\\mathrm{Gal}}(L|k), \\text{with $\\ker(.\\vert_L) = \\mathop{\\mathrm{Gal}}(K|L)$},\\\\\n        &\\Leftrightarrow  \\text{by isomorphism theorem } \\mathop{\\mathrm{Gal}}(L|k) \\cong \\frac{G}{\\mathop{\\mathrm{Gal}}(K|L)}.\n    \\end{split}",
        "hash": "1e2a24ac1e0c1242",
        "id": "eq-1149",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "◻\n:::\n\nWe can now start to show Grothendieck's reformulation of Galois theory\nwhich focuses on the absolute Galois group and sets equipped with a\ncontinuous and transitive action.\n\n::: {#separable_closure .definition}\n**Definition 53**. We define the **separable closure** of",
        "hash": "26d877a77991b2ec",
        "id": "eq-1150",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "in",
        "hash": "582967534d0f909d",
        "id": "eq-1151",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "as the compositum of all separable extensions of",
        "hash": "437560f476bbdee9",
        "id": "eq-1152",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ". And\nwe call",
        "hash": "3367571b31727035",
        "id": "eq-1153",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {

        "canonical_tex": ".\nWe have shown essential surjectivity.\\\nThe last statement is now direct from Corollary\n[55](#Galois_normal_reformulation){reference-type=\"ref\"\nreference=\"Galois_normal_reformulation\"}. ◻\n:::\n\n#### Étale and Separable Algebras\n\nWe end this section with an important generalisation of the previous\nreformulation theorem, which makes use of *étale algebras*, a natural\nreplacement for finite separable extensions (for commutative algebras).\nIt allows one to consider sets with a continuous but not necessarily\ntransitive",

        "id": "eq-1342",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "into a product of fields\nand an element",
        "hash": "3fa5c758ba3afdee",
        "id": "eq-1343",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", the maps",
        "hash": "f47b0f6d8498ce03",
        "id": "eq-1344",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "induces the injection of exactly one",
        "hash": "d48ecf3a007f1346",
        "id": "eq-1345",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "in",
        "hash": "582967534d0f909d",
        "id": "eq-1346",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ". Indeed, if",
        "hash": "8ad1967dc072927a",
        "id": "eq-1347",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", being a field extension,",
        "hash": "c6f7cdf3807a81c6",
        "id": "eq-1348",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "injects into",
        "hash": "b0f7019662c067e2",
        "id": "eq-1349",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ",\nand on the other hand, a product",
        "hash": "3e9b7e284018f4d8",
        "id": "eq-1350",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "cannot inject into",
        "hash": "ce6916ba765ea39a",
        "id": "eq-1351",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "since",
        "hash": "6b5a3ded016ab782",
        "id": "eq-1352",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "has no zero-divisors. Thus we have the decomposition",
        "hash": "0918f5002fc63ef2",
        "id": "eq-1353",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ".\nFor a similar reason, given another finite étale",
        "hash": "b0a7cb80411bcfa4",
        "id": "eq-1354",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "-algebra",
        "hash": "6989a0a06e38caea",
        "id": "eq-1355",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", a morphism",
        "hash": "5ec589a20c9fd22d",
        "id": "eq-1356",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is given by a\ncollection of morphisms",
        "hash": "c2be5a5e151b1094",
        "id": "eq-1357",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", for each",
        "hash": "66cb1ee3667bba94",
        "id": "eq-1358",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ". And these correspond bijectively to morphisms of the\ncorresponding",
        "hash": "11ff9e35273b2954",
        "id": "eq-1359",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "-sets by the previous theorem. ◻\n:::\n\nÉtale algebras will also play an important role later in this thesis.\nFor that reason, we give another characterisation of finite étale",
        "hash": "391430a019f501af",
        "id": "eq-1360",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "-algebras. For that, we first need the next lemma.\n\n::: {#finite_dimensional_direct_sum_reduced .lemma}\n**Lemma 59**. *A finite-dimensional commutative algebra",
        "hash": "40b56550ce0dc88c",
        "id": "eq-1361",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "over a field",
        "hash": "7875c6c08e2344eb",
        "id": "eq-1362",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is isomorphic to a direct sum of finite field extensions of",
        "hash": "48de45b10a82a81e",
        "id": "eq-1363",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "if\nand only if",
        "hash": "ebdb88b1bfed1328",
        "id": "eq-1364",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is reduced.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* The ''only if\\\" part is obvious, one just has to notice that\nfields are already reduced.\\\nTo prove the other direction, by decomposing",
        "hash": "9fef7bdb03e7bd58",
        "id": "eq-1365",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "into a finite direct\nproduct of indecomposable",
        "hash": "12a85bd3e955fe8d",
        "id": "eq-1366",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "-algebras, we may assume that",
        "hash": "5a11f047d16ff724",
        "id": "eq-1367",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is\nindecomposable. Under this restriction",
        "hash": "9e7f4daa57be8f6e",
        "id": "eq-1368",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "can have no idempotent\nelements other than",
        "hash": "fef99b54344ecdd1",
        "id": "eq-1369",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "and",
        "hash": "6201111b83a0cb5b",
        "id": "eq-1370",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", indeed, if",
        "hash": "91c1493ca0780f73",
        "id": "eq-1371",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is an\nidempotent, then",
        "hash": "2c4c7e088f558b86",
        "id": "eq-1372",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "would be a non-trivial\ndirect product decomposition since",
        "hash": "3c285cde5ecb8c3a",
        "id": "eq-1373",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ". The lemma follows\nif we show that every non-zero element",
        "hash": "e94de248b203224e",
        "id": "eq-1374",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is invertible making it\na field. Since",
        "hash": "1614da2a47af396f",
        "id": "eq-1375",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is finite-dimensional, it is Artinian, i.e. the\ndescending chain of ideals",
        "hash": "978e194fd74500fa",
        "id": "eq-1376",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "must\nstabilise. And thus for some",
        "hash": "579a2f20c2e34b69",
        "id": "eq-1377",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", we have",
        "hash": "4145f0ff85f4612f",
        "id": "eq-1378",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "for some",
        "hash": "ea5bc48ceb98effc",
        "id": "eq-1379",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ". By iteration we get",
        "hash": "0251fd5fef27dc02",
        "id": "eq-1380",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "for",
        "hash": "10c22bcf4c768b51",
        "id": "eq-1381",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "until",
        "hash": "2e3200de84b9cada",
        "id": "eq-1382",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", thus",
        "hash": "1ab38411881b9b22",
        "id": "eq-1383",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", an idempotent. If",
        "hash": "03b4276394abeeb7",
        "id": "eq-1384",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ", then",
        "hash": "aae687415b646286",
        "id": "eq-1385",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "which is a contradiction\nsince",
        "hash": "a3951c58f9487d63",
        "id": "eq-1386",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "by assumption. So",
        "hash": "b3f9fb2bdce94ecb",
        "id": "eq-1387",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "and",
        "hash": "6201111b83a0cb5b",
        "id": "eq-1388",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is invertible.",
        "hash": "b5e02ba0329c8ae2",
        "id": "eq-1389",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is reduced. ◻\n:::\n\n::: {#etale_algebras .theorem}\n**Theorem 60**. *Let",
        "hash": "544462ce35616d8e",
        "id": "eq-1390",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "be a finite-dimensional commutative",
        "hash": "7652ad764ff4a760",
        "id": "eq-1391",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "-algebra. Then the following are equivalent :*\n\n- *",
        "hash": "f95dbc4fb6e47489",
        "id": "eq-1392",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is étale*\n\n- *",
        "hash": "9fab99107c694bb4",
        "id": "eq-1393",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "*\n\n- *",
        "hash": "129008d3b838348e",
        "id": "eq-1394",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "is reduced.*\n:::\n\n::: proof\n*Proof.* Let us first show that",
        "hash": "369e6f8f9f5f247f",
        "id": "eq-1395",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ":\\\nWe may restrict to finite separable extensions",
        "hash": "37b04729c6cc75f4",
        "id": "eq-1396",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "of",
        "hash": "28391d3bc64ec15c",
        "id": "eq-1397",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": ". Then of\ncourse, we have",
        "hash": "594bee19cb7f93e7",
        "id": "eq-1398",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "for some polynomial",
        "hash": "29ac3d20850938c2",
        "id": "eq-1399",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {
        "canonical_tex": "in",
        "hash": "582967534d0f909d",
        "id": "eq-1400",
        "mathml": null,
        "section_id": null,
        "semantic_tag": "other"
      },
      {

        "hash": "be945c4e46e3aeae",

        "canonical_tex": "\\begin{split}\n          \\mathop{\\mathrm{ev}}(\\rho_{V\\otimes V^*}(g)(v\\otimes f)) &= \\mathop{\\mathrm{ev}}(\\rho_V(g)(v)\\otimes \\rho_{V^*}(g)(f))\\\\\n          & = \\rho_{V^*}(g)(f(\\rho_V(g)(v))) \\\\\n          & = f(\\rho_V(g^{-1})(\\rho_V(g)(v))) \\\\\n          & = f(\\rho_V(g^{-1}g)(v))\\\\\n          & = f(v) = \\mathop{\\mathrm{ev}}(v\\otimes f)\n      \\end{split}",

      {
        "canonical_tex": "\\begin{split}\n          \\rho_{V^*\\otimes V}(g)(\\mathop{\\mathrm{coev}}(1)) = \\rho_{V^*\\otimes V}(g)\\Bigl(\\sum^n_{i=1} e^i\\otimes e_i\\Bigr) & = \\sum^n_{i=1}\\rho_{V^*}(g)(e^i)\\otimes \\rho_V(g)(e_i)\\\\\n          & =\\sum^n_{i=1} \\Bigl( \\sum_{j=1}^n g^{-1}_{ji} e^n\\Bigr)\\otimes \\Bigl(\\sum^n_{l=1}g_{il}e_j\\Bigr) \\\\\n          &= \\sum_{i=1}^n\\sum_{j=1}^n\\sum_{l=1}^n g^{-1}_{ji}g_{il}(e^j\\otimes e_l)\\\\\n          & = \\sum^n_{j=1}\\sum^n_{l=1}(\\delta_{jl}(e^j\\otimes e_l)) = \\sum^n_{i=1} e^i\\otimes e_i\n      \\end{split}",

      {

        "id": "thm-1",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Definition 1. A homotopy of paths in $X$ starting at $x_0$ and ending at $x_1$ is a family of paths $\\gamma_t:[0,1]\\rightarrow X$ indexed by $I$ such that - the endpoints are fixed : $\\gamma_t(0) = x_...",

        "id": "thm-2",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Definition 2. A continuous map $f:X\\rightarrow Y$ is called a homotopy equivalence if there exists a continuous map $g:Y\\rightarrow X$ such that $g\\circ f \\simeq \\mathop{\\mathrm{id}}_X$ and $f\\circ g\\...",
        "type": "definition"
      },
      {
        "depends_on": [],
        "id": "thm-3",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Definition 3. The fundamental group of $X$ based at $x$, denoted by $\\pi_1(X,x)$, is the set of homotopic classes of loops based at $x$.",
        "type": "definition"
      },
      {
        "depends_on": [],
        "id": "thm-4",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Remark 1. Let $f:(X,x)\\rightarrow (Y,y)$ be a continuous map between pointed topological spaces such that $f(x)=y$, then we denote by $f_:\\pi_1(X,x)\\rightarrow\\pi_1(Y,y)$ the induced homomorphism, obt...",
        "type": "remark"
      },
      {
        "depends_on": [],
        "id": "thm-5",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Proposition 4. Homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental groups. If $f:X\\rightarrow Y$ is a homeomorphism, then $f_ :\\pi_1(X,x)\\rightarrow \\pi_1(Y,f(x))$ is an isomorphism.*",
        "type": "proposition"
      },
      {
        "depends_on": [],
        "id": "thm-6",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Proof. If $f$ is a homeomorphism, then $(f^{-1})_\\circ f_ = (f^{-1}\\circ f)_ = (id_X)_ = id_{\\pi_1(X,x)}$. Similarly, $f_ \\circ (f^{-1})_$ is the identity on $\\pi_1(Y,f(x))$. ◻",
        "type": "proof"
      },
      {
        "depends_on": [],
        "id": "thm-7",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Corollary 5. Two homotopic equivalent spaces have the same fundamental group. If $f:X\\rightarrow Y$ is a homotopy equivalence, then $f_ :\\pi_1(X,x)\\rightarrow \\pi_1(Y,f(x))$ is an isomorphism.*",
        "type": "corollary"
      },
      {
        "depends_on": [],
        "id": "fund_grou_base_pt",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Proposition 6. If $X$ is a path-connected topological space, then $\\pi_1(X, x_0)$ and $\\pi_1(X, x_1)$ are isomorphic for any $x_0,x_1\\in X$.",
        "type": "proposition"
      },
      {
        "depends_on": [],
        "id": "thm-9",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Proof. Since two points $x_0$ and $x_1$ may be joined by a path $\\gamma$ starting at $x_0$ and ending at $x_1$, $\\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is non-canonically isomorphic to $\\pi_1(X,x_1)$ via $\\delta \\mapsto \\gamm...",
        "type": "proof"
      },
      {
        "depends_on": [],
        "id": "thm-10",
        "section_id": "sec-2-1",
        "statement": "Example 7. Of course, since $\\mathbb{R}^n$ is contractible, any loop is homotopic to the constant loop, so $\\pi_1(\\mathbb{R}^n,x) = \\{1\\}$ for any base point $x\\in\\mathbb{R}^n$.",

Subsets of\n`α` are modelled as predicates `α → Prop`.  This is a self-contained restatement\nof *topological space*, so the file depends only on the Lean 4 core library. -/\nstructure Topology (α : Type w) where\n  IsOpen : (α → Prop) → Prop\n  isOpen_univ : IsOpen (fun _ => True)\n  isOpen_inter : ∀ u v, IsOpen u → IsOpen v → IsOpen (fun a => u a ∧ v a)\n  isOpen_iUnion : ∀ {ι : Type w} (u : ι → α → Prop),\n      (∀ i, IsOpen (u i)) → IsOpen (fun a => ∃ i, u i a)\n\n/-- `f : Y → X` is continuous when the preimage of every open set is open. -/\ndef Continuous {X Y : Type w} (tX : Topology X) (tY : Topology Y) (f : Y → X) : Prop :=\n  ∀ u, tX.IsOpen u → tY.IsOpen (fun y => u (f y))\n\n/-- The quotient topology that a topology on `Y` induces on `Quotient s`: a set\nis open exactly when its preimage under the canonical projection is open. -/\ndef quotientTopology {Y : Type w} (tY : Topology Y) (s : Setoid Y) :\n    Topology (Quotient s) where\n  IsOpen V := tY.IsOpen (fun y => V (Quotient.mk s y))\n  isOpen_univ := tY.isOpen_univ\n  isOpen_inter _ _ hu hv := tY.isOpen_inter _ _ hu hv\n  isOpen_iUnion u hu := tY.isOpen_iUnion (fun i y => u i (Quotient.mk s y)) hu\n\n/-- **Lemma 13 (universal property of the topological quotient / lift).**\nLet `X` and `Y` be topological spaces and let `s` be an equivalence relation\n(a `Setoid`) on `Y`.  If `p : Y → X` is continuous and constant on\n`s`-equivalence classes (`y ≈ y' → p y = p y'`), then there is a *unique* map\n`g : Quotient s → X` that is continuous for the quotient topology and factors\n`p` through the canonical projection, i.e. with `g ∘ Quotient.mk s = p`.\n(The `∃!`/\"there is a unique\" is spelled out explicitly as existence together\nwith a uniqueness clause, since the bare `∃!` notation lives in Mathlib.) -/\ntheorem univ_ppty_lift\n    {X Y : Type w} (tX : Topology X) (tY : Topology Y) [s : Setoid Y]\n    (p : Y → X) (hp : Continuous tX tY p)\n    (hcompat : ∀ y y' : Y, y ≈ y' → p y = p y') :\n    ∃ g : Quotient s → X,\n      (Continuous tX (quotientTopology tY s) g ∧ g ∘ Quotient.mk s = p) ∧\n        ∀ g' : Quotient s → X,\n          (Continuous tX (quotientTopology tY s) g' ∧ g' ∘ Quotient.mk s = p) →\n            g' = g := by\n  refine ⟨Quotient.lift p hcompat, ⟨?_, ?_⟩, ?_⟩\n  · -- the lift is continuous: its preimages coincide with those of `p`\n    intro u hu\n    exact hp u hu\n  · -- the lift genuinely factors `p` through the projection\n    funext y\n    rfl\n  · -- any continuous map factoring `p` coincides with the lift\n    rintro g ⟨-, hg⟩\n    funext q\n    exact Quotient.inductionOn q (fun a => congrFun hg a)\n\nend GrokRxiv\n",

summary — claude-haiku-4-5 pass 
{
  "audience": "Graduate students in algebraic geometry, students of Galois theory, and mathematicians seeking to understand Grothendieck's conceptual innovations connecting topology and algebraic geometry.",
  "key_contributions": [
    "Systematic exposition of the analogy between topological covering spaces and Galois theory, demonstrating how both encode symmetries through profinite groups.",
    "Construction and detailed study of the étale fundamental group for schemes, including comparison with the topological fundamental group via transcendental methods for complex varieties.",
    "Unified treatment of fundamental groups through Tannakian duality, showing how étale, topological, and motivic Galois groups arise naturally within a single categorical framework.",
    "Self-contained development of category-theoretic foundations (functors, limits, adjunctions, abelian categories) necessary for modern algebraic geometry."
  ],
  "plain_language_summary": "This thesis presents a systematic exploration of how fundamental groups—objects that capture the essential structure of spaces and their symmetries—appear across three major mathematical domains. The work begins with classical topological covering spaces, where fundamental groups classify how spaces can be continuously wrapped around themselves. It then follows Grothendieck's revolutionary insight that similar ideas apply to algebraic varieties, the geometric objects defined by polynomial equations. However, standard topological methods fail for varieties because they lack sufficient structure; the solution is the étale topology, a combinatorial framework where covering spaces are replaced by certain algebraic morphisms. Through this lens, the étale fundamental group emerges as the algebraic analogue of its topological cousin, and remarkably, the two coincide when the variety is complex—a deep connection bridging algebra and analysis. Finally, the thesis reveals that all three versions of the fundamental group—topological, étale, and motivic—are unified through Tannakian duality, a principle that recovers groups as symmetry groups of fiber functors on monoidal categories of representations.",
  "tldr": "A thesis developing fundamental groups as a unifying framework across topology, algebraic geometry via étale theory, and linear algebra through Tannakian duality."
}
